 © 2026 Yahoo. All rights reserved. Listen up, because this is the most important piece of advice you're going to receive as we head into Week 8 of the college football season. 
 If you find yourself at a stadium and somehow luck into a sideline pass or a premium seating area near the benches or end up in one of those crazy field-rush situations, there is absolutely one thing you must keep in mind.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Do not engage with players.
 Don't trash talk them. Don't touch them. Don't flip them the middle finger. And if you somehow do any of those things, understand that cameras are everywhere and there's no place to hide anymore. 
 What are the odds that Saturday will mark the third straight week with an embarrassing incident between fan and player that causes someone to get banned for life? Probably pretty good given the way too many athletic departments have let their sidelines get out of control with celebrities, influencers, big donors, various hangers-on and lickspittles who have been incorrectly conditioned to think social media anonymity works in real life. 
 Add all that to a buildup of liquid courage over an intense 3 1/2-hour football game and you inevitably get some yokel who couldn't bench press a flower vase running up to a 250-pound defensive end carved out of granite, thinking they can say or do something provocative without consequence. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement They should consider themselves lucky if all they get out of it is a lifetime ban rather than a trip to the hospital. 
 Seriously, what the heck is going on here? 
 First came the Alabama fan two weeks ago, who was captured on video slapping the helmet of Georgia linebacker Raylen Wilson before shoving him away with one hand while the other held a styrofoam cup. 
 This particular fan was sitting in the very first row, near where Georgia players were celebrating with friends and family, and Wilson initially thought it was a Georgia fan congratulating him, which is partly why he walked away without a confrontation. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement But once the video began to circulate, and it became clear that this was an Alabama fan who was acting maliciously, the school identified and banned him for life from attending any other athletic events. 
 "It's disappointing behavior by any fan," Georgia coach Kirby Smart said.
 With the amount of attention that story got, particularly around the SEC, you'd think everyone would get the message.
 But in the aftermath of Florida's victory at Texas last week, a young fan wearing a burnt orange windbreaker was standing about three feet from a group of Gators when he looked right at 6-foot-6, 277-pound LJ McCray and flipped him the bird. Then, this "fan" continued to hold up his right middle finger while filming with his other hand. As a group of Florida players started to follow him, staffers stepped in to make sure the situation didn't escalate. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Maybe the craziest part of all is that this dummy was smiling through the whole thing, acting as if he's protected from anything bad that might happen to him. While we in no way condone violence or players retaliating — we've seen that before and it goes poorly for everyone — these so-called fans do not realize how little sympathy they would engender if they walked away with a few bruises. 
 Texas athletic director Chris Del Conte apologized in his weekly newsletter and said the matter had been addressed internally. He later told the Houston Chronicle that the offender was a local college student who attends an out-of-state university. 
 "Having access to our field comes with a responsibility to represent Texas with class and respect," Del Conte wrote. "This individual failed to uphold that responsibility and has been permanently banned from Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium."
 The more troubling part, according to a post on X by the Houston Chronicle's Kirk Bohls, was that Del Conte "doesn't know who authorized a field pass for the young student." 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement While there certainly should be an audit trail linked to every field pass just for general safety and security reasons, it's not that far-fetched to come up with a scenario where a big donor who has access to a few passes gives a couple to his buddy who gives one to their snot-nosed kid who ends up acting like an idiot toward a player because their entire life has been awash in privilege and entitlement. 
 Thanks to social media, we see a lot of this in our world now. In so many everyday interactions, Main Character Syndrome has become the norm and shame is on the decline. Rather than engaging with the rules of a polite society, too many people want to treat their march through life as an opportunity to make content.
 And that's dangerous for college sports because there has never really been much desire to erect a solid wall between player and fan. 
 Whether they want to admit it or not, athletic departments are in the business of selling access. For the right price, you can sit where you want, stand on the sideline, text suggestions to the coaches, maybe even get into the locker room. It's why schools have stuffed premium seats into areas that used to be empty and why they pay a lot of money for a coach to show up for an hour at a local sports bar to take questions from radio callers.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Despite the explosion of money and fame in college sports, there is still a closeness and community part of fandom that you don't get in the NFL or NBA. 
 Why do schools still pay coaches a lot of money to show up for an hour at some local sports bar and take questions from radio callers? Why are local businesses eager to hand out NIL deals that often require players to make in-person appearances or sign autographs? Why do schools allow field-storming after big wins when they know they'll pay a hefty fine and potentially put athletes in danger? 
 Allowing people to feel like they can reach out and touch the program is a feature, not a bug. 
 But occasionally, it does come with a downside. And if these incidents start happening on a more regular basis, it will need to be systematically addressed for the sake of the players who are expected to take the abuse of opposing fans from close range and not retaliate. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement That's not sustainable. 
 Yeah, everyone loves the images of students coming out of the stands to celebrate and tearing down goalposts after a big win. It's a part of the experience that differentiates college from the pros. But as college sports becomes more professionalized, it's fair to ask whether the field of play needs to be treated more as a workplace.
 Players and coaches shouldn't have to worry that the aftermath of a game is going to turn into a melee because someone who doesn't belong on the field in the first place did something to provoke a player whose emotions were already on edge.
 After the issues we've seen the last couple weeks, that's a fair concern. Expecting players to have restraint 100 percent of the time when fans lose their inhibitions seems like a bad bet. After all, it's only going to take one ugly incident to make a school look culpable for allowing that kind of access in the first place.
